query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a two‐phase coexistence simulation using ab initio molecular dynamics can provide accurate predictions of the melting temperature, latent heat (reflected in entropy and enthalpy of fusion) and the volume change at melting, while avoiding the high computational cost of full thermodynamic integration.
generation.material_initial_state: A simulation cell prepared with coexisting solid and liquid regions of the material at conditions near the melting point.
generation.intervention: Perform an ab initio two‐phase coexistence molecular dynamics simulation where the solid and liquid phases are allowed to equilibrate.
generation.conditions: Run the simulation in an appropriate statistical ensemble (e.g., NPT) at pressures and temperatures near the suspected melting point using a sufficiently large simulation cell to minimize interfacial effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The solid–liquid interface, whose stability and dynamics mediate the phase transition and allow for determination of equilibrium conditions.
generation.mechanism: By directly simulating a system with both phases, the equilibrium temperature (where neither phase grows at the expense of the other) is identified as the melting point. Concurrently, calculations of energy and volume differences between the solid and liquid regions yield the enthalpy and entropy of fusion as well as the volume change at melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: The simulation will converge to an equilibrium temperature corresponding to the melting point. Energy and volume analyses of the two phases during coexistence will produce estimates of the enthalpy/entropy of fusion and the volume change upon melting that agree within the uncertainty margins with those obtained by full ab initio free-energy integration.
generation.baseline: The traditional ab initio free-energy approach using thermodynamic integration based on DFT results.
generation.boundary: This method is expected to perform reliably for materials where interfacial dynamics do not dominate (i.e., where the interface is well-behaved) and where simulation sizes are adequate to reduce finite-size effects. In cases of extremely sluggish kinetics or very small simulation cells, the method may introduce additional uncertainty.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties arise from finite-size effects, the dynamics of the solid–liquid interface, and the simulation time required to reach equilibrium. Quantitative accuracy may vary based on the specifics of the material system and simulation parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare an ab initio two‐phase coexistence molecular dynamics simulation for a refractory material with an experimentally known melting point. Measure the equilibrium temperature, energy, and volume differences between the coexisting phases. Compare these results with those from high-accuracy free-energy integration methods and experimental data.
measurements: Energy difference between the coexisting solid and liquid phases (to infer enthalpy of fusion)
Volume difference between the phases (volume change at melting)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the two‐phase coexistence method yields a melting temperature, latent heat, or volume change that deviates from the benchmark values (from established thermodynamic integration methods or experiments) by more than the estimated uncertainty, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.
